extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of natural philosophy, evolutionary theory, and comparative geology/biology (general scientific readership)
extracted.subtask_description: A chapter-length exposition arguing the general law that homogeneous masses and states are unstable and tend to become heterogeneous across physical, chemical, biological, and mental domains, with illustrative examples from nebular theory, planetary rings, Earth's cooling, chemistry, organismal development, species variation, and mental classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instability of a finite diffused mass (general physical principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any finite mass of diffused matter, even vast enough to form our whole sidereal system, could not be in stable equilibrium; in default of absolute sphericity, absolute uniformity of composition, and absolute symmetry of relation to all external forces, its concentration must go on with an ever-increasing irregularity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: small initial irregularities will be amplified because motion once set up becomes a cause of subsequent motion in that direction; local aggregations concentrate to their own centres of gravity and, due to resistance of the medium, motions become curvelinear and compose into rotation of the incipient sidereal system. Conclusion used to account for observed galactic and stellar patchiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detached rotating rings cannot remain homogeneous
rubrics_metrics.description: A rotating spheroid which detaches an equatorial ring cannot maintain that ring in absolute uniformity; to preserve equilibrium the ring would need almost perfect uniformity in the action of all external forces, which is immensely improbable; therefore rupture and subdivision into many parts will occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laplace assumed rupture at one point collapsing the ring; but the text argues a vast nebulous ring with feeble cohesion must break up into many parts, and once separation begins, grouping accelerates until aggregation into single masses occurs. External disturbing forces inevitably destroy any equilibrium among separated masses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Homogeneous celestial relations are unstable (orbits and rings)
rubrics_metrics.description: The homogeneous relation (e.g., concentricity of Saturn and its rings; perfect circular orbits) is unstable and would gravitate into a heterogeneous one; mutual perturbations generate eccentricities and destroy perfect symmetrical arrangements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observed persistence of Saturn's rings does not contradict because solid/liquid cohesion and exceptional symmetrical forces of outer rings can maintain continuity; nevertheless mathematical proofs indicate concentricity/homogeneity would not remain if perfect, illustrating the general doctrine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cooling and crust formation as consequence of instability
rubrics_metrics.description: The cooling and solidification of the Earth's surface (formation of a crust) is a necessary consequence of the instability of the homogeneous: exposure of different parts to different conditions leads a uniform mass to pass into a multiform state (e.g., polar vs equatorial contrasts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because different parts of Earth's surface are unequally exposed to the chief external centre of force (the Sun), main divisions are unequally modified as the crust thickens and cools, producing the present large-scale contrasts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chemical differentiation tied to decreasing temperature and complexity
rubrics_metrics.description: As the Earth cooled, the simplest, most stable compounds (protoxides, alkalies, earths) formed first; more complex compounds are less stable and form later, so chemical heterogeneity increases as temperature decreases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General law: other things equal, stability decreases as complexity increases; illustrated by ordering from protoxides → deutoxides/tritoxides → salts → hydrated salts → supersalts/double salts → complex organic compounds (albumen, fibrine), which decompose at much lower temperatures. The proposition is statistical/average, not absolute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meteorologic processes illustrate destruction of homogeneity
rubrics_metrics.description: Meteorologic processes ultimately set up in the Earth's atmosphere exemplify the destruction of a homogeneous state produced by unequal exposure to incident forces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Named as further consequences of the general law without specification in this passage; offered as another domain where unequal incident forces produce heterogeneity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiation of organismal parts arises from unequal exposure
rubrics_metrics.description: In a mass of organizable matter (e.g., germ or lowest living forms), outer and inner parts are differently related to surrounding agencies (nutriment, oxygen, stimuli), and unequal exposure of parts to such forces leads to destruction of original equilibrium and to differentiation of parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two outcomes: (1) disturbing forces may overbalance affinities causing decomposition, or (2) more commonly, they modify organic compounds so that the most exposed parts are most modified. Examples: protozoa with little differentiation due to uniform exposure; sponges with indefiniteness because of uniform currents; fixed organisms or those with definite attitudes exhibit surface differentiation corresponding to exposure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surface-vs-interior primary differentiation in development
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary differentiation in embryonic development is between exterior and interior: peripheral cells often coalesce into a membrane (blastoderm) and the surface becomes unlike the centre because of differing exposures to incident forces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This differentiation does not occur simultaneously over the whole surface but starts at one place and spreads. Secondary differentiation follows: the superficial portion divides into two layers (serous/ectoderm and mucous/endoderm) according to which parts contact surrounding agents vs internal yolk—i.e., differentiation corresponds to contrasts of conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of the instability principle: heredity and specific form
rubrics_metrics.description: The instability-of-homogeneous principle supplies no key to detailed phenomena of organic development—generic and specific peculiarities (why different eggs become different species) must be ascribed to hereditary transmission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author notes possibility that hereditary differences themselves may be accumulated results of repeated exposure-based modifications over generations; but acknowledges that specific hereditary mechanisms remain unexplained by the simple instability principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Species lapse into heterogeneity due to different aggregates of forces
rubrics_metrics.description: Within a species, individuals are never quite alike and tend to produce varieties; this lapse from homogeneity to heterogeneity is caused by members being subjected to unlike sets or aggregates of circumstances (forces).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence: varieties more numerous where conditions depart widely from original ones (cultivation/domestication). Whether natural selection acts wholly or partly is irrelevant to the deduction that differences of environment produce differentiation; survival and multiplication of varieties indicate harmony with specific aggregates of forces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental evolution as subdivision from homogeneous consciousness
rubrics_metrics.description: States of consciousness originally homogeneous become heterogeneous through differences in the changes wrought by different forces; mental development (e.g., visual classification) proceeds by forming subdivisions and more refined classes as perceptive organs improve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustration: earliest visual classifications distinguish merely light vs darkness, then stationary vs moving, then nearer vs remote, then shapes as retina subdivides; each refinement multiplies divisions and sharpens class boundaries, showing mental differentiation parallels physical/biological instability of homogeneous.
